tldr: The authors propose Motus2, a world model that handles action generation, future prediction, and value evaluation with a single set of shared weights. They show that large-scale egocentric data and a reinforcement learning loop enable self-evolving dexterous multi-finger manipulation.
hero_caption: Overall architecture and learning/inference loop of Motus2. A single shared backbone acts as policy (WAM), simulator (AC-WM), and evaluator (VM), forming a closed loop that evaluates predicted outcomes of generated candidate actions to achieve self-evolution.
overview:
Imitation learning has long been the dominant approach for dexterous robot manipulation. However, collecting successful demonstrations on real hardware is extremely expensive. Furthermore, imitation learning alone cannot learn from failures or suboptimal motions to assess what was good or bad and autonomously improve the policy. Hand occlusions and contact ambiguity also pose significant challenges.

To tackle these issues, the authors developed Motus2, a world model based on a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) with a single set of shared parameters. The key idea is that one model serves three roles: action proposal (policy), visual outcome prediction (simulator), and progress evaluation (evaluator). During inference, it enables Best-of-$N$ planning to pick the top action. During training, it continuously updates the policy via model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) based on DiffusionNFT. Crucially, curated successful demonstrations are used for action imitation, while failed and suboptimal trajectories are fully leveraged for dynamics modeling and value learning.

The authors systematically evaluated the pipeline, spanning pre-training on large-scale monocular and stereo egocentric data, robot domain adaptation, and tactile feedback integration. On real-robot evaluations, pre-training and intermediate training drastically boosted success rates (from 0% for the WAN baseline to 84% for Motus2). Combining MBRL and test-time planning brought even further performance gains.
contributions: Integrating three control interfaces—policy, simulator, and value evaluator—into a single shared-weight model, establishing an autonomous policy improvement loop (self-evolution).
Building a staged data scaling recipe that adapts from large-scale monocular and stereo egocentric data to real-robot data, and demonstrating scaling laws for stereo data.
Realizing a framework that effectively utilizes not only successful demonstrations but also failed and suboptimal interaction data as supervision signals for dynamics prediction and value learning.
Demonstrating high-frequency hand action correction and prediction via a tactile expert, alongside a working memory mechanism that captures long-term dependencies on real physical systems.

sections.heading: Beyond imitation learning: The path to a self-evolving world model
sections.summary: Dexterous manipulation demands more than mapping the latest observation to an action; it requires maintaining history, reasoning about contact, and improving autonomously. This paper presents Motus2, a world model that unifies action proposal, future prediction, and value evaluation in a single model.
sections.details:
Robotic foundation models have heavily relied on imitation learning across human-curated datasets with action labels. However, collecting demonstrations on real robots is exceptionally costly. Imitation learning alone lacks mechanisms to evaluate whether an action is good or bad, or to refine policies from the consequences of its own actions.

This makes human egocentric data an appealing source of physical prior knowledge. Monocular data provides broad coverage of tasks and hand-object interactions, while synchronized stereo data offers depth and precise 3D hand poses. Transferring these priors to dexterous robot manipulation, however, requires handling hand occlusions (partial observability) as well as subtle contact dynamics like fingertip slipping and grasp formation that vision alone struggles to resolve.

Motus2 addresses these challenges across two dimensions: data scaling and model scaling. On the model side, a single shared model serves three roles: policy (World–Action Model), simulator (Action-Conditioned World Model), and evaluator (Value Model). The policy proposes candidate actions, the simulator forecasts their visual consequences, and the evaluator assesses task progress, completing a closed loop for self-evolution. A major strength is that failed interactions are not discarded; they are fully utilized for learning dynamics and value estimation.

sections.heading: Where world models, egocentric priors, and MBRL converge
sections.summary: The authors situate Motus2 at the intersection of general world models (GWM), egocentric priors for dexterous manipulation, and world model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL).
sections.details:
World models in robot control generally fall into three categories: policies that generate actions, simulators that predict future observations conditioned on actions, and evaluators that score outcomes. The prior Motus model proposed a UniDiffuser-style joint video-action model, but it did not include an autonomous improvement loop. Motus2 advances this by integrating a value evaluator and MBRL within the same unified model.

Dexterous multi-finger manipulation requires coordinating discontinuous contact dynamics. Human egocentric data, as seen in H-RDT and EgoVLA, provides strong priors. Still, visual information alone cannot resolve the ambiguities of contact-rich tasks, making tactile reactive control and morphological alignment essential.

Recent post-training work for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models explores policy improvement using world model rollouts. Yet, how to couple action decision-making, world simulation, and value estimation within a single model—and how to make successful, failed, and suboptimal data mutually reinforce each other—remained an open question. Motus2 provides a direct answer.

sections.heading: One set of weights for three roles: Motus2 architecture and training
sections.summary: Formulating tasks as language-instructed POMDPs, Motus2 extracts a policy, simulator, and evaluator from one model via causal masking and loss gating, coupled with DiffusionNFT-based MBRL, working memory, and a lightweight tactile expert.
sections.details:
3.1 Overview
The task is treated as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). Given an observation context $c_t$, the joint distribution over an executable action chunk $A_t$, future latent visual observations $Z_t$, and discretized task progress values $Y_t$ is causally decomposed (Action-first) as $p(A_t, Z_t, Y_t \mid c_t) = \pi_\theta(A_t \mid c_t) \cdot p_\theta(Z_t \mid c_t, A_t) \cdot p_\theta(Y_t \mid c_t, A_t, Z_t)$.

3.2 General World Modeling
While pre-training uses bidirectional attention across video and actions, robot adaptation introduces an Action-first mask. Action tokens cannot attend to future video or value tokens within their chunk, future video tokens can attend to actions, and read-only value query tokens can attend to both. Furthermore, supervision signals are routed according to data quality. Only high-quality successful demonstrations supervise action generation, whereas failed and suboptimal trajectories are routed exclusively into simulator (future prediction) and evaluator (value prediction) modes. This allows the model to learn physics and evaluation criteria efficiently without imitating undesirable behaviors.

3.3 Value-Guided Closed-Loop Self-Evolution
The evaluator learns relative task progress (positive progress in 0–1, and -1 for failed or irrelevant actions). At inference time, Best-of-$N$ planning executes the candidate action with the highest predicted value. During training, DiffusionNFT translates evaluator scores into Flow Matching update gradients for the policy. Candidate actions scoring higher than the batch mean are pushed toward a positive implicit velocity field, while lower-scoring ones are pushed in the negative direction. This training runs efficiently via an asynchronous pipeline implemented with Ray.

3.4 Working Memory
To address partial observability such as hand occlusions, three history retention strategies are compared: the default Sliding Window, Global Autoregression (maintaining the KV cache of full history), and Hybrid Memory (MemoryWAM style, keeping high-resolution initial and recent frames while compressing intermediate frames into latent tokens).

3.5 Tactile Expert
To support high-frequency contact feedback without repeatedly executing the heavy backbone, the authors introduce a lightweight tactile expert. Using an intermediate action chunk denoised once to a mid-noise level by the backbone and its KV cache, the expert applies fine-grained action adjustments based on immediate tactile signals. Self-supervised learning that predicts post-action contact forces is also incorporated to heighten contact sensitivity.

sections.heading: A 130k-hour egocentric data pyramid: Monocular, stereo, and real robot
sections.summary: A massive ~130,000-hour egocentric dataset was constructed. The pipeline applies standardized hand keypoints and 'BoxTrim', an automated processing step that filters out rapid head movements, creating high-quality multimodal data.
sections.details:
The training dataset follows a pyramid structure built from web video, monocular and stereo egocentric data, human-robot morphological alignment data, and tactile-equipped real-robot trajectories.

Monocular data provides extensive task and semantic diversity, while stereo data contributes depth cues and precise 3D hand poses. To utilize both, a unified 134-dimensional hand representation was introduced, encompassing translation, rotation, and 20 fingertip joint positions for both hands.

To clean noisy long-form egocentric video, the authors developed BoxTrim, a quality-aware temporal processing pipeline. It adaptively computes thresholds based on instantaneous wrist movement to discard frames with rapid head turns, and automatically trims segments where dual-hand tracking is lost. In addition, vision-language models were used to annotate detailed environment, overall action, and left/right hand descriptions. Pre-training scales up systematically from visual representation learning on monocular video (Stage 1: 840k steps) to joint stereo-action training (Stage 2: 450k steps).

captions.F4: The egocentric data pyramid and semantic diversity of the corpus. The hierarchy ranges from web video to stereo egocentric and real-robot data (left), alongside a rich distribution of annotated action verbs, objects, tasks, and scenes (right).

sections.heading: Putting the world model to the test: Scaling, MBRL, and tactile sensing
sections.summary: Across five real-robot manipulation tasks, the authors extensively evaluated the contributions of egocentric pre-training, stereo scaling laws, MBRL and planning gains, memory mechanisms, and tactile feedback.
sections.details:
5.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations used a dual-arm system with 20-DoF multi-finger hands across five tasks demanding precise alignment and sustained contact: Insert Ball, Place Phone, Mount Eraser, Screw Bulb, and Multi-Finger Coordinated Grasping. Each task had 20–25 initial configurations, and success rate (SR) was measured under strict all-or-nothing completion criteria.

5.2 Main Results
Without pre-training (WAN baseline), the success rate was 0%. Monocular and stereo pre-training (Pretrain-SFT) lifted the macro-average success rate to 51%. Motus2 after robot-domain intermediate training (Midtrain-SFT) achieved 84%, scoring 100% on Insert Ball and Mount Eraser, and 90% on Screw Bulb, substantially outperforming $\pi_{0.5}$.

5.3 Scaling Laws for Stereo Egocentric Data
Evaluating subsets of 2k, 4k, 10k, and 20k hours revealed a clear log-linear scaling law ($\mathcal{L} = 0.101 - 0.005 \cdot \ln(D)$), where prediction error on held-out human actions decreased linearly against log dataset size.

5.4 Model-Based Policy Improvement and Planning
Starting from baseline Motus2 (65.0%), adding test-time planning reached 67.5%, applying MBRL via DiffusionNFT reached 72.5%, and combining both reached 75.0%. Because the evaluator accurately detects failed trajectories with negative progress, action selection and policy updates reinforce each other.

5.5 Long-Horizon Context Mechanisms
On exploratory tasks with severe occlusions, Global Autoregression (preserving full history) was compared with Hybrid Memory (compressed tokens). Global Autoregression proved far superior: 78% vs 52% in simulation average, and 57.5% vs 25% on real robots. This suggests that token compression discards fine-grained visual details.

5.6 Tactile Feedback
On tasks requiring delicate force modulation, such as Unstack Cup and Tear Paper, introducing the tactile expert improved success rates from 60.0% to 72.5% (+12.5 points), confirming its efficacy in contact-rich fine manipulation.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A foundational general world model for self-evolving manipulation
sections.summary: Motus2 unifies action generation, world simulation, and outcome evaluation into a single model, enabling self-evolution through closed-loop reinforcement learning. Combining massive egocentric data with real-robot adaptation lays a foundation for dexterous manipulation.
sections.details:
This work establishes Motus2 as a self-evolving general world model for multi-finger dexterous manipulation. Rather than stitching together separate modules, the core breakthrough is that a single model with shared weights serves as policy, simulator, and evaluator. This keeps candidate proposal, outcome prediction, value assessment, and policy updating within a self-contained decision-and-learning loop.

On the data side, the paper validates treating human egocentric data as a massive source of physical interaction priors, progressively adapting it from monocular to stereo and finally to real robots. Structuring the training so dynamics and values are learned from failed as well as successful data is highly practical in data-constrained robotics settings. Along with tactile sensing integration, Motus2 provides a concrete blueprint for self-evolving robot foundation models.

sections.heading: Open challenges: The tactile hardware gap and future frontiers
sections.summary: The main limitation lies in tactile transferability due to morphological differences between human and robot hands. Future work includes aligning hand geometries and integrating longer-horizon multimodal foundation models.
sections.details:
The primary limitation identified by the authors is the scalability of cross-embodiment learning with wearable tactile sensors. Glove-based tactile sensors suffer from internal strain and fabric-on-fabric contact noise during finger motion, making it hard to isolate true external contacts. More fundamentally, modern dexterous robot hands are not isomorphic to human hands; robotic pinkies are often longer, and fingers are thicker. Consequently, tactile data collected with human gloves cannot be directly transferred to robot hands, posing a morphological barrier.

Future directions include developing anthropomorphic hands that bridge this geometric gap, as well as novel full-hand tactile materials. On the modeling side, the authors point toward incorporating stronger video generation backbones and unified multimodal models, fully fusing vision, language, action, tactile feedback, and value estimation to support longer-horizon prediction and autonomous self-improvement.

sections.heading: Appendix: Robot platforms, data collection, and retargeting details
sections.summary: The appendix details three dual-arm dexterous robot platforms used in experiments, workspace-referenced human-robot alignment collection, and the optimization algorithm retargeting MediaPipe keypoints to multi-finger hand joints.
sections.details:
The appendix covers hardware and algorithmic specifics of the experimental systems.

Real-Robot Setups (Appendix A)
Three dual-arm setups were evaluated: a Tianji Marvin dual-arm with 20-DoF Wuji hands (equipped with ZED cameras and tactile gloves), a Tianji Gento Luna dual-arm with Wuji Hand 2, and another Luna dual-arm with 22-DoF Sharpa Wave hands.

Human-Robot Alignment Data Collection (Appendix B)
Human operators wore tactile gloves and wrist-mounted HTC VIVE Trackers, with a third Tracker fixed to the workbench as a workspace reference frame. This established stable base-invariant wrist trajectories alongside synchronized stereo video capture.

Hand Retargeting (Appendix D)
An inverse kinematics (IK) optimization algorithm maps 21 3D hand keypoints (MediaPipe format) from egocentric data into the 20-DoF joint space of the Wuji hand. The objective combines a full-hand posture loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{full}}$) and a fingertip pose loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tip}}$) critical for grasping, dynamically balancing their weights based on distances between the thumb and other fingertips.

takeaways: Integrating policy, simulator, and evaluator into a single shared-weight model via attention masks is both elegant and effective, avoiding fragmented multi-model pipelines.
Routing failed and suboptimal trajectories into simulator dynamics and evaluator training—rather than throwing them away—is a practical strategy that dramatically boosts data efficiency.

Stereo egocentric video exhibits a clear log-linear scaling law with respect to dataset size, demonstrating that massive human video pre-training directly translates into dexterous manipulation capability.

For long contexts, current token-compressed hybrid memories lose critical fine-grained features; paying the computational cost for full-history global autoregression provides substantially higher real-robot success rates.
limitations: Morphological differences between human and robot hands (finger length, thickness, geometry) still hinder direct cross-embodiment transfer of wearable tactile data.
Global autoregression incurs linearly growing KV cache and attention computation as episode length increases, creating computational bottlenecks for real-time control.

Simulating future video rollouts and running value evaluations for planning and MBRL remains computationally heavy, requiring extensive pipeline optimization to manage latency during real-world deployment.
